arguments.court_reasoning: The Court recognized the States' margin of appreciation in organizing judicial systems and court jurisdictions.

arguments.claim: The Court held it is not its function to compare different decisions of national courts and must respect their independence, except in cases of evident arbitrariness.

anchor.surface_text: The Chamber considered that it was not its function to compare different decisions of national courts, even if given in apparently similar proceedings; it must respect the independence of those courts.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court limits its review to arbitrariness and respects domestic courts' independence.

arguments.claim: The Court found that conflicting decisions between ordinary administrative courts and the Supreme Military Administrative Court existed, resulting in different legal treatment of similar cases.

anchor.surface_text: Diametrically opposite conclusions were thus reached by the ordinary administrative courts (Ankara Administrative Court and Supreme Administrative Court) and the Supreme Military Administrative Court.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court acknowledged the existence of conflicting case-law between different courts.

arguments.claim: The Court held that the mere finding of a conflict of case-law is not sufficient to constitute a violation of Article 6; the impact on fair trial and legal certainty must be assessed.

anchor.surface_text: The mere finding of a conflict of case-law is not sufficient in itself to constitute a violation of Article 6 of the Convention.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court balances the existence of conflict with its impact on fairness and legal certainty.

arguments.claim: The Court found that the conflicting decisions resulted from failure of courts to respect jurisdiction boundaries, causing conflict of jurisdiction between ordinary administrative courts and the Supreme Military Administrative Court.

anchor.surface_text: This reveals a conflict of jurisdiction between these two types of court which were called upon to give judgment, in parallel, on the same legal issue.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court identified jurisdictional overlap as the origin of conflicting decisions.

arguments.claim: The Court noted that the Jurisdiction Disputes Court ruled that the Supreme Military Administrative Court had jurisdiction in such cases, and the 4th Chamber of the Ankara Administrative Court referred to this ruling when declining jurisdiction.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court recognized the role of the Jurisdiction Disputes Court in settling jurisdiction conflicts.

arguments.claim: The Court found that despite the Jurisdiction Disputes Court rulings, ordinary administrative courts continued to accept and rule on similar cases, failing to respect jurisdiction boundaries.
arguments.court_reasoning: The Court noted the failure of ordinary courts to comply with jurisdiction rulings.

arguments.claim: The Court emphasized that the role of the Jurisdiction Disputes Court is not to resolve conflicts of case-law but only exceptional conflicts of judgments where enforcement of a right is impossible.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court clarified the limited scope of the Jurisdiction Disputes Court's role.

arguments.claim: The Court held that in a system with several Supreme Courts not subject to a common hierarchy, it cannot demand a vertical review mechanism to harmonize case-law.

anchor.surface_text: While such considerations obtain where the conflicting decisions arise within a hierarchical judicial structure, they cannot be transposed to the present case.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court recognized structural differences in judicial systems affecting case-law consistency.

arguments.claim: The Court considered that the lack of a common regulatory authority shared by the Supreme Courts capable of establishing uniform interpretation is not a breach of the Convention.
arguments.court_reasoning: The Court noted that multiple supreme courts without a harmonizing authority is common and not a violation.

arguments.claim: The Court held that conflicting case-law may be tolerated without undermining legal certainty in systems with multiple Supreme Courts existing side by side.

anchor.surface_text: In a judicial system like that of Turkey, with several different branches of courts, and where several Supreme Courts exist side by side and are required to give interpretations of the law at the same time and in parallel, achieving consistency of the law may take time, and periods of conflicting case-law may therefore be tolerated without undermining legal certainty.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court accepted that temporary conflicting case-law is tolerable in such systems.

arguments.claim: The Court emphasized that interpretation is inherent in judicial work and divergences between courts are inevitable outcomes of interpreting legal provisions.

anchor.surface_text: Interpretation is inherent in the work of the judiciary. However clearly drafted a legal provision may be, there is an inevitable element of judicial interpretation.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court recognized judicial interpretation as natural and divergences as inevitable.

arguments.claim: The Court considered that the Supreme Administrative Court and the Supreme Military Administrative Court have the possibility to settle divergences themselves by respecting jurisdiction boundaries or adopting the same approach.
arguments.court_reasoning: The Court expects domestic supreme courts to manage divergences internally.

arguments.claim: The Court held that it is not its role to act as a fourth instance to review domestic courts' interpretation or conflicting decisions unless there is evident arbitrariness.

anchor.surface_text: Just as it is not for the Court to act as a court of third or fourth instance and review the choices of the domestic courts concerning the interpretation of legal provisions and the inconsistencies that may result, nor is it its role, it would like to emphasise, to intervene simply because there have been conflicting court decisions.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court limits its review to arbitrariness and does not intervene for mere conflicts.

arguments.claim: The Court found that the interpretation made by the Supreme Military Administrative Court was not arbitrary, unreasonable or affecting fairness, but a case of application of domestic law.

anchor.surface_text: The interpretation made by the Supreme Military Administrative Court of the facts submitted to it for examination cannot be said to have been arbitrary, unreasonable or capable of affecting the fairness of the proceedings, but was simply a case of application of the domestic law.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the military court's interpretation was within its jurisdiction and not arbitrary.

arguments.claim: The Court found that the decision of the 4th Chamber of the Ankara Administrative Court that it did not have jurisdiction was not arbitrary.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the 4th Chamber's jurisdiction decision consistent with law and not arbitrary.

arguments.court_reasoning: The majority found the military court's decision was within its discretion and not arbitrary.

arguments.claim: The dissenting judges argued that the Jurisdiction Disputes Court's rulings were theoretical and ineffective as ordinary administrative courts continued to accept similar cases.

anchor.surface_text: However, the resolution by the Jurisdiction Disputes Court of the conflict between the two courts was theoretical and illusory.

arguments.court_reasoning: The majority acknowledged the rulings but accepted the system's tolerance of conflicting decisions.

arguments.claim: The dissenting judges concluded that the malfunctioning of conflict settlement machinery and inconsistent court decisions caused a violation of the right to a fair hearing under Article 6.

anchor.surface_text: Consequently, we consider that a violation of the right to a fair hearing was caused by a malfunctioning of the machinery set in place to settle conflicts of jurisdiction, coupled with inconsistency in court decisions concerning cases having their origin in the same factual situation.

arguments.court_reasoning: The majority did not accept this conclusion, finding no violation.

FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT

Holds, by ten votes to seven, that there has been no violation of Article 6 7 1 of the Convention.

Done in English and in French, and delivered at a public hearing in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 20 October 2011.

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found conflicting decisions between ordinary administrative courts and the Supreme Military Administrative Court but held that such divergences, given the independence of courts and absence of arbitrariness, did not violate Article 6 7 1. The Court emphasized respect for domestic courts' independence, the margin of appreciation in judicial organisation, and that conflicting case-law may be tolerated without undermining legal certainty in systems with multiple supreme courts.

holdings.text: The interpretation made by the Supreme Military Administrative Court of the facts submitted to it for examination cannot be said to have been arbitrary, unreasonable or capable of affecting the fairness of the proceedings, but was simply a case of application of the domestic law.

anchor.surface_text: ...the interpretation made by the Supreme Military Administrative Court of the facts submitted to it for examination cannot be said to have been arbitrary, unreasonable or capable of affecting the fairness of the proceedings, but was simply a case of application of the domestic law.

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found the military court's interpretation was within its jurisdiction and not arbitrary, thus not violating the fairness requirement of Article 6 7 1.

holdings.text: The decision of the 4th Chamber of the Ankara Administrative Court that it did not have jurisdiction in the applicants' case was not at all arbitrary.

anchor.surface_text: ...that in the circumstances of the present case the decision of the 4th Chamber of the Ankara Administrative Court that it did not have jurisdiction in the applicants' case was not at all arbitrary.

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found the 4th Chamber's jurisdiction decision consistent with law and not arbitrary, thus no violation of Article 6 7 1 on this ground.
